name: Crackhead Control to Carni
summary: Changing from Crackhead Control toward Carni requires opening the second-leg clinch, isolating an arm, clearing the head-side leg and establishing the shoulder-lock angle.
description: Changing from Crackhead Control toward Carni requires opening the second-leg clinch, isolating an arm, clearing the head-side leg and establishing the shoulder-lock angle.
overview:
The bottom guard player begins in Crackhead Control, facing a top player whose posture is controlled. Crackhead Control alone does not isolate the required arm. The reviewed Carni lesson begins from Z guard through Jersey, so this multi-stage connection remains conditional.

Use the guard and shoulder connection to bring the opponent close before moving the high leg. Manage the shoulder and neck line with a forearm frame as the leg clears the head. Turn partly belly down with the knee close and foot supported rather than wrenching the leg across the head.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Richie Martinez — Carni shoulder lock from Z guard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iClQ2Np-n30).

Carni is a rotational lock on the shoulder: the triceps control and head-side leg clamp constrain the arm as the bottom player changes angle. Establish that shoulder configuration gently after opening Crackhead Control, and release before a forced roll.

attacker.description: Crackhead Control to Carni (attacker): Use the guard and shoulder connection to bring the opponent close before moving the high leg. Manage the shoulder and neck line with a forearm frame as the leg clears the head.
attacker.overview:
The bottom guard player begins in Crackhead Control, facing a top player whose posture is controlled. Crackhead Control alone does not isolate the required arm. The reviewed Carni lesson begins from Z guard through Jersey, so this multi-stage connection remains conditional.

Use the guard and shoulder connection to bring the opponent close before moving the high leg. Manage the shoulder and neck line with a forearm frame as the leg clears the head. Turn partly belly down with the knee close and foot supported rather than wrenching the leg across the head.

Keep the captured arm connected so the opponent cannot freely roll or withdraw the shoulder. Hold the wrist and elbow at a comfortable angle; a small change can load the shoulder rapidly. Release the wrist and leg clamp immediately on a tap or when the partner needs to roll safely.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Use the inside neck frame to control incoming chest pressure while hip movement creates the angle for the head-side leg to clear. The new shoulder clamp is a submission entry with its own triceps control, not the result of merely lowering one of the Crackhead legs.

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): What must be added beyond the two-leg posture clinch?
flashcards.answer: Crackhead reinforcement does not supply Carni's arm isolation; the shoulder clamp requires its own setup.
flashcards.answer_line: Separate isolation of an opposing arm

plausible: Only a tighter cross of the high feet
Only a higher pull on the opponent's head
trap: Only a hip turn with both opposing arms still free

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): What blocks forward chest pressure while the leg clears?
flashcards.answer: The inside neck-side forearm maintains room as the high leg clears the head.
flashcards.answer_line: A forearm frame at the side of the neck

plausible: A wrist lying outside the opponent's chest
Both hands pulling the ankle toward you
trap: A forearm pushing the captured elbow straight

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): Which hip position supports the new shoulder clamp?
flashcards.answer: Martinez anchors through the hips and supported foot, drawing the knee close while turning partly belly down.
flashcards.answer_line: Partly belly down, knee close, foot supported

plausible: Flat on the back with the knee flared away
Turned onto the hip with the foot floating
trap: Belly down with the knee extended away from the chest

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): Which movement does the retained triceps grip directly obstruct?
flashcards.answer: The triceps connection retains the upper arm and limits rolling or shoulder withdrawal from the Carni clamp.
flashcards.answer_line: Free shoulder withdrawal or an unopposed roll

plausible: Bending the captured elbow while the shoulder stays pinned
Moving the free arm toward an inside frame
trap: Tucking the chin while the upper arm stays captured

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): What should the first shoulder-capture drill omit?
flashcards.answer: Rehearse the arm capture and supported angle without adding wrist leverage into a shoulder finish.
flashcards.answer_line: Wrist leverage that rotates the fixed shoulder

plausible: The forearm barrier while clearing the leg
The supported foot beside the shoulder clamp

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): Your partner must roll to relieve the shoulder; what releases?
flashcards.answer: Release wrist and leg control before a necessary roll; do not hold the shoulder fixed while the body turns.
flashcards.answer_line: Both wrist control and the leg clamp

plausible: Only your hand support beside the head
Only the butterfly hook below the hips
trap: Only the wrist while keeping the upper arm clamped

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): Which limb must the new clamp contain?
flashcards.answer: The new submission entry is a shoulder clamp with a retained upper arm, not a lower-body capture.
flashcards.answer_line: The opponent's upper arm at the shoulder

plausible: The forearm with the shoulder outside the leg
The neck with the target upper arm released
trap: Both wrists with neither upper arm retained

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): What intervening controls are required before the shoulder lock?
flashcards.answer: The direct combination remains conditional: establish arm isolation, head clearance and the Carni angle separately.
flashcards.answer_line: Arm isolation and head-side leg clearance

plausible: Only dropping the second high leg
Only breaking posture with both legs high
trap: Only turning the shoulder while the head stays trapped

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): The leg catches behind the head during your turn; what now?
flashcards.answer: If the head blocks the leg, preserve the frame and adjust the hip angle rather than forcing the foot across.
flashcards.answer_line: Pause and reopen space with the forearm and hips

plausible: Pull the foot across without changing the hip angle
Pull the wrist while the head still blocks the leg
trap: Keep turning belly down before the leg clears

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (bottom): Which contact anchors the shown Carni position against posture?
flashcards.answer: The demonstrated Carni uses the supported foot and close knee to anchor the shoulder, after the head-side leg has cleared.
flashcards.answer_line: Supported foot and knee close to the shoulder

plausible: An unsupported foot held high with the knee wide
The foot on the mat with the knee drifting away
trap: The knee close with the foot still behind the head

defender.description: Crackhead Control to Carni (defender): A leg clearing the head with an overhook is an upper-body trap, even if a butterfly hook remains below. Avoid reaching away while the opponent sets the triceps control.
defender.overview:
The bottom guard player begins in Crackhead Control, facing a top player whose posture is controlled. Crackhead Control alone does not isolate the required arm. The reviewed Carni lesson begins from Z guard through Jersey, so this multi-stage connection remains conditional.

A leg clearing the head with an overhook is an upper-body trap, even if a butterfly hook remains below. Avoid reaching away while the opponent sets the triceps control. Maintain a balanced base and a safe inside frame before the shoulder becomes clamped.

Create slack around the shoulder and elbow before moving the hips past the legs. Do not force a forward roll when the triceps and wrist are fixed; tap if pressure has already engaged. Raise the head and chest only after the arm and head-side leg are clear.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Make the early escape before the triceps grip and head-side leg immobilize the shoulder. Keep the upper arm aligned while the connection opens; posture recovery begins after that release.
key_principles: Identify the shoulder threat: A leg clearing the head with an overhook is an upper-body trap, even if a butterfly hook remains below.
Keep the elbow close early: Avoid reaching away while the opponent sets the triceps control.
Deny the belly-down angle: Maintain a balanced base and a safe inside frame before the shoulder becomes clamped.
Free the arm before passing: Create slack around the shoulder and elbow before moving the hips past the legs.
Avoid rolling against the lock: Do not force a forward roll when the triceps and wrist are fixed; tap if pressure has already engaged.
Rebuild posture after release: Raise the head and chest only after the arm and head-side leg are clear.

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (top): A leg clears your head while an overhook holds you; what is threatened?
flashcards.answer: Recognize the shoulder-lock setup even when a lower butterfly hook remains.
flashcards.answer_line: Your shoulder in a leg-assisted clamp

plausible: Your neck enclosed beneath an under-chin shin
Your elbow extended across a high leg fulcrum
trap: Your wrist bent without restraint on the upper arm

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (top): Before triceps control closes, where should the elbow stay?
flashcards.answer: Avoid reaching away while the opponent establishes triceps control; keep the arm compact before the clamp closes.
flashcards.answer_line: Beside the ribs, in the inside space

plausible: Extended away toward the far hip
Behind the torso as you turn away

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (top): What preserves inside forearm space before the shoulder clamp closes?
flashcards.answer: Use an early inside frame and balance before the leg and triceps immobilize the shoulder.
flashcards.answer_line: An inside frame with a balanced base

plausible: A wrist grip with the forearm outside the chest gap
A chest lift with the elbow left across the high leg
trap: A wide floor post with the upper arm reaching away

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (top): What must clear before your hips move past the legs?
flashcards.answer: Create slack and free the shoulder and elbow before treating the exchange as a pass.
flashcards.answer_line: The shoulder-and-elbow connection to the clamp

plausible: Only the lower butterfly hook
Only the opponent's supporting foot from the mat
trap: Only a gap beside the opponent's waist

flashcards.question: Crackhead to Carni (top): Why can a forward roll fail with wrist and triceps fixed?
flashcards.answer: Do not roll against a fixed wrist and triceps. Obtain release, or tap if the shoulder lock is engaged.
flashcards.answer_line: The clamped shoulder cannot follow the roll

plausible: The triceps grip slips off as soon as your hips rise
The lower hook absorbs the rotation instead of the shoulder
trap: The wrist follows the torso while the triceps remain clamped
